run.runNote: Phase 1 Step 1-2 (source exploration + candidate extraction query generation only; no CodeQL execution, no compile, no LLM labeling in this round) against the flask-cors_vuln source tree. WORKFLOW.md confirms Pass 1 = CWE-022/023/036/073 Path Traversal with pass query name Pass1_PathTraversal.ql. The CodeQL database flask-cors-db sits INSIDE the source tree, so all exploration, file traversal, and evidence collection excluded flask-cors-db (only codeql-database.yml and read-only git inventory of the snapshot commit were used for metadata/scope). The database sourceLocationPrefix matches the explored tree (creation sha 5c6e05e), so file/line evidence below refers to the same snapshot the database was built from; the git ls-tree inventory of sha 5c6e05e confirms the database snapshot contains exactly the 28 .py files observed on disk. The audit target is the Flask-Cors library itself (version 3.0.8), a pure CORS response-header filtering Flask extension/middleware: it reads a small set of HTTP request values (Origin / Access-Control-Request-Method / Access-Control-Request-Headers headers, request.path, request.method), matches them against developer-supplied CORS options (decorator kwargs / app.config CORS_* keys), and writes CORS response headers. The library performs NO filesystem access of any kind: all 5 package modules (core.py, decorator.py, extension.py, __init__.py, version.py - 731 lines) were read in full and contain zero open/os/pathlib/shutil/io calls. The ONLY filesystem operations in the entire database snapshot are three literal-path builtin open() reads in setup.py (packaging script) plus constant-derived os.path.dirname/abspath and sys.path.insert import-path hacks in the 3 examples and docs/conf.py. The untrusted-input boundary is therefore exclusively the HTTP request surface (Flask 'request' proxy), which flows into string/regex matching and response-header construction - never into a file path.

target.projectDescription: Flask-Cors 3.0.8 (flask_cors/version.py:1 __version__ = '3.0.8') - a Flask extension adding CORS (Cross Origin Resource Sharing) support. Two entry points: (1) the cross_origin decorator (flask_cors/decorator.py:18) wrapping a Flask view function - wrapped_function (decorator.py:121) computes merged options via get_cors_options(current_app, _options), calls the view f(*args, **kwargs) (Flask URL rule variables pass through these wrapper args), wraps the result with make_response and applies set_cors_headers; (2) the CORS extension class (flask_cors/extension.py:16) - init_app (extension.py:131) merges app.config CORS_* keys (get_app_kwarg_dict core.py:303) with constructor/kwargs options, parses resource regexes (parse_resources core.py:66) and registers cors_after_request via app.after_request (extension.py:154), which matches request.path against each resource regex (extension.py:178, try_match core.py:275) and calls set_cors_headers. set_cors_headers (core.py:224) reads request.headers/request.method (core.py:245) and delegates to get_cors_headers (core.py:176), which reads the Origin header (request_headers.get('Origin') core.py:177), the preflight Access-Control-Request-Method/Access-Control-Request-Headers headers (core.py:194/:203) and writes the CORS response headers (resp.headers.add core.py:250). All path-like values (request.path, resource regexes) are used ONLY as regex match subjects - never to locate, open, read or write files.

inputBoundaryInventory.summary: The audit target is a Flask extension library, so the untrusted-input boundary is exclusively the HTTP request, accessed through the Flask 'request' proxy: (1) the Origin request header - request_headers.get('Origin') at core.py:177 inside get_cors_headers (request_headers = request.headers passed from set_cors_headers core.py:245) - the dominant attacker-controlled string, matched against the configured origins via try_match/try_match_any (core.py:128/:271-285) and echoed back into the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header (core.py:133/:184, resp.headers.add core.py:250); (2) the preflight headers Access-Control-Request-Method (request_headers.get(ACL_REQUEST_METHOD) core.py:194) and Access-Control-Request-Headers (request_headers.get(ACL_REQUEST_HEADERS) core.py:203, split on ',' and matched per-header in get_allow_headers core.py:161-173) - echoed into response headers; (3) request.path (extension.py:178/:180) - the URL path matched against resource regexes with try_match/re.match - a path-shaped attacker string, but used purely as a regex match subject, never as a filesystem path; (4) request.method (core.py:245, decorator.py:125) - 'OPTIONS' preflight detection; (5) the wrapper boundaries where Flask route variables (URL rule captures) pass through library code: wrapped_function(*args, **kwargs) decorator.py:121 and extension.py:160 forwarding them to the user's view f (and cors_after_request(resp) extension.py:171 / set_cors_headers(resp) extension.py:224 receiving the response object whose headers may embed request-derived values set by the view); (6) developer/operator-level configuration - cross_origin(*args, **kwargs) decorator.py:18, CORS.__init__(app, **kwargs) extension.py:126, init_app(app, **kwargs) extension.py:131, get_cors_options(appInstance, *dicts) core.py:288 and the app.config CORS_* reads app_config.get(k) core.py:311/:313 in get_app_kwarg_dict - the person embedding flask-cors in an app is the same trust domain as the options they configure: OPERATOR-trust, emitted for the labeling step to classify, NOT automatically attacker sources. NO other boundary exists: no uploads/multipart, no JSON/form/args/cookies reads, no archive entries, no subprocess output, no environment variables, no CLI, no DB, no message queue (verified by full read of the 5 package modules plus greps over the whole non-excluded tree). The filesystem-operation side is correspondingly minimal: the package contains ZERO filesystem calls; the entire snapshot contains only setup.py open(join(dirname(__file__), 'flask_cors/version.py'), 'r') :15, open(join(dirname(__file__), 'requirements.txt'), 'r') :18 and open('README.rst') :29 (all literal, plus exec(f.read()) :16 - code-execution of the just-read local file, Pass 4 material), the constant-derived os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))) + os.sys.path.insert(0, parentdir) import-path hack in the 3 examples (:17-18) and sys.path.insert(0, os.path.abspath('..')) in docs/conf.py:21. No path-validation guards exist anywhere because no configurable path exists - there is nothing to traverse from inside the library.

uncoveredCases: Flask 'request' proxy aliasing: request_attr rows are matched on the syntactic base name 'request' (from flask import request in core.py:20/decorator.py:13/extension.py:11); an alias import (from flask import request as req) or a request passed under another local name would be missed - not observed in this tree (every module imports the bare name).

request_headers / acl_request_headers / options / _options / app_config matching is likewise name-anchored to the exact parameter/variable names used in this codebase; a renamed variable would be missed (not observed). The dict-comprehension app_config.get(k) rows (core.py:311/:313) are inside a comprehension scope - still matched as ordinary Call nodes.

serialize_option(options_dict, key) reads its values via the options_dict[key] SUBSCRIPT (core.py:334-336), not .get - subscript-on-local-name reads were not given a family in this project (config-only channel, operator-trust); recorded here so the labeling step knows the config_field family under-covers it by one shape.

Flask's URL-rule variable binding (path variables -> view kwargs) happens inside the flask library (external, not in this database); the wrapper_param rows (decorator.py:121 / extension.py:160 wrapped_function *args/**kwargs) are the in-repo boundary where those values pass through library code, but the actual binding site is invisible to this extraction - the rows anchor the channel, and the star-parameter arg_index values are the syntactic positions (0/1) rather than concrete route-variable indices.

The bare-name join/dirname matching is constrained to setup.py because the from-import form (`from os.path import join, dirname`, setup.py:13) leaves no syntactic receiver to anchor on; a bare join()/dirname() call in another file of a different project would be missed unless that file has the same import - not observed elsewhere in this snapshot. The os.path.join attribute form is also matched (0 rows expected here) for cross-project recall.

os.sys.path.insert (examples:18) resolves sys through the os module attribute - matched via a two-level attribute chain (os.sys.path.insert); any other exotic spelling of the sys.path list access would be missed (none observed).

Dynamic-dispatch ambiguity is minimal in this snapshot: the only name-based member matches are .get (anchored to request_headers/resp.headers/options/_options/app_config receivers), .insert (anchored to a *.path receiver whose object is sys), and the os/os.path attribute forms; no same-named members on unrelated receivers were observed in non-excluded files (headers.add in core.py:184/:250 and f.required_methods.add in decorator.py:118 use .add, not .insert, and are not matched).
